construct_or_mutation: 162-residue B. subtilis IIAGlc domain of the glucose permease, uniformly 15N-labeled (>95%), expressed in E. coli, about 0.8 mM
other_conditions: tumbling: tm = 6.24 ± 0.01 ns (global fit); S2 mostly 0.75-0.90; N-terminal residues I2-G11 and Q32 have negative NOEs; A3 NOE = -6.7 ± 0.7 attributed to amide proton exchange; double-timescale fit for I2, L6, N8, G11, E12, E13, Q32 (Table I); per-residue table in Supplement; related structures: crystal (Liao et al. 1991) and NMR (Fairbrother et al. 1992a) structures cited, no PDB ids given
timescale: te < ca. 25 ps for most residues; te > ca. 50 ps for I2-E13 and Q32; no Rex broadens a 15N line by more than 2 Hz (per-residue model-free fit; single-timescale for most, double-timescale for 7 residues)
caveat_note: Sheet lists 298.5 K (no BMRB entry); the paper recorded at 308 K, pH 6.6, 500 MHz, so the temperature differs from the sheet value. Table I and the supplement table are garbled in the extracted text, so per-residue S2, te and Rex were not copied. Dynamics for the N-terminal tail and possibly Q32 are qualitative only because amide proton exchange may bias their NOEs.
experiment: 15N T1, T2 and {1H}-15N NOE at 500 MHz (proton frequency) with model-free analysis (S2, te, Rex, tm), 137 of 151 protonated backbone amides
author_claim: Most residues are rigid (S2 0.75-0.90, te under ca. 25 ps); the N-terminal residues 1-13, the loop P25-D41 whose apex lies next to the active site, and A146-S149 are more mobile.
anchor: Residues found to be more mobile than the average were concentrated in three areas: the N-terminal residues (1-13), which were observed to be highly disordered
